title: Set Matrix Zeroes — first row/column as markers.
shortTitle: Set Matrix Zeroes — using the first row and column as in-place markers

s1_definition.profdef: Setting matrix zeroes means that if any cell in an m-by-n matrix is zero, its entire row and entire column must be set to zero, and the challenge is to do it in place using only constant extra space. The efficient technique reuses the matrix's own first row and first column as marker storage that records which rows and columns must be zeroed, plus two boolean flags to remember whether the first row and first column themselves originally contained a zero.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a grid where each cell is a daily profit figure for a branch, and a zero means that branch was flagged as frozen for that day. Policy says if any single day is frozen, the whole branch (its column) and the whole day (its row) must be wiped to zero for the audit. Instead of keeping a separate notepad of which branches and days to wipe, Priya scribbles the flags in the margin of the grid itself — the top row and the left column — then wipes everything in one careful pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use the first row and first column as your zero-marker notepad so you need only constant extra memory to blank out every flagged row and column.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Setting matrix zeroes means that if any cell in an m-by-n matrix is zero, its entire row and entire column must be set to zero, and the challenge is to do it in place using only constant extra space. The efficient technique reuses the matrix's own first row and first column as marker storage that records which rows and columns must be zeroed, plus two boolean flags to remember whether the first row and first column themselves originally contained a zero.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a grid where each cell is a daily profit figure for a branch, and a zero means that branch was flagged as frozen for that day. Policy says if any single day is frozen, the whole branch (its column) and the whole day (its row) must be wiped to zero for the audit. Instead of keeping a separate notepad of which branches and days to wipe, Priya scribbles the flags in the margin of the grid itself — the top row and the left column — then wipes everything in one careful pass.

**One line to remember:** Use the first row and first column as your zero-marker notepad so you need only constant extra memory to blank out every flagged row and column.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive solution copies the matrix or keeps separate sets of row and column indices, costing O(m + n) or more extra space. The in-place trick removes that extra space by storing the markers inside the matrix.

First we scan to answer two questions with boolean flags: does the first row contain any zero, and does the first column contain any zero. These two flags are needed because we are about to overwrite the first row and column with markers, so we must remember their original state separately.

Then we iterate over the inner matrix, from row 1 and column 1 onward. Whenever we find `matrix[i][j] == 0`, we set `matrix[i][0] = 0` and `matrix[0][j] = 0`. This writes a marker into the left column and top row saying "this row must be zeroed" and "this column must be zeroed".

Next we iterate the inner matrix again. For each inner cell, if its row marker `matrix[i][0]` is zero or its column marker `matrix[0][j]` is zero, we set the cell to zero.

Finally we handle the first row and first column using the two flags we saved at the start. If the first-row flag was true, we zero the entire first row; if the first-column flag was true, we zero the entire first column. The whole algorithm is O(m times n) time and O(1) extra space.

A senior nuance: the order matters. You must apply the inner cells before zeroing the first row and column, otherwise you destroy the markers before using them. The two saved flags must be computed before you start writing any markers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India holds a reconciliation grid where rows are dates and columns are branches, each cell a settled amount. A zero means a discrepancy was detected at that date and branch. Risk policy says a single discrepancy quarantines the whole date and the whole branch, so every amount on that date and every amount for that branch must be blanked to zero before the report is filed.

This is exactly how set matrix zeroes works. A single zero cell propagates to its entire row and entire column.

Problem 2 — The grid can be huge and memory on the batch server is tight, so we cannot afford to allocate a full second matrix or large index sets just to remember what to blank.

This is exactly why we reuse the first row and first column as in-place markers, keeping the extra memory to two boolean flags regardless of how large the grid grows.

The code will have an `Account` class for domain flavor, a `ReconciliationGrid` class with a `quarantineZeroes` method implementing the in-place algorithm, and a runnable demo that prints the grid before and after with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 3-by-4 grid with zeroes at row 0 column 2 and at row 2 column 1.

Step 1: We scan the first row and find a zero at column 2, so `firstRowHasZero` becomes true. We scan the first column and find no zero, so `firstColHasZero` stays false.

Step 2: We scan the inner matrix from row 1, column 1. The only inner zero is at row 2 column 1, so we set `matrix[2][0] = 0` (row marker) and `matrix[0][1] = 0` (column marker).

Step 3: We scan the inner matrix again. Row 2 has its marker set, so every inner cell in row 2 becomes zero. Column 1 has its marker set, so every inner cell in column 1 becomes zero.

Step 4: Because `firstRowHasZero` is true, the whole first row becomes zero. Because `firstColHasZero` is false, the first column keeps whatever the markers produced.

Final output:


sections.s6_takeaway:
Set matrix zeroes is a problem where, if any cell in the matrix is zero, I must set that cell's entire row and entire column to zero, and the interesting constraint is to do it in place using only constant extra space. The naive approach keeps separate sets of row and column indices, which costs extra memory proportional to the dimensions, and the elegant approach avoids that by reusing the matrix's own first row and first column as the marker storage.

The algorithm has four careful phases. First I record, in two boolean flags, whether the first row and the first column originally contained any zero, because I am about to overwrite them with markers and I must not lose their original state. Second I scan the inner matrix and, for each zero I find, I write a zero into that row's position in the first column and that column's position in the first row, which marks the row and column for blanking. Third I scan the inner matrix again and zero any cell whose row marker or column marker is set. Fourth I use the two saved flags to decide whether to blank the first row and the first column themselves.

The order is the part that trips people up. If I zeroed the first row and column before using the markers, I would destroy the information I need, so I always apply the inner cells first and the border last, and I always compute the two flags before writing any marker. The whole thing runs in time proportional to the number of cells with only constant additional memory.

In my project at National Bank of India, we had a reconciliation grid where rows were dates and columns were branches, and a zero meant a detected discrepancy that policy required us to quarantine across the whole date and the whole branch before filing. Because the batch server had tight memory, the in-place marker technique let us process very large grids without allocating a second matrix, which kept the nightly reconciliation job within its memory budget.
